prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and active form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the one candidate on which all six of us converged in first place, and the convergence is justified on the merits. The chain runs from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, through the identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its insulinotropic and satiety actions in humans, to long-acting agonists with documented glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit. It is original, mechanistically complete, independently confirmed in large trials and of very large clinical and public-health reach. The work is mature and recognition is timely. I keep the basic-discovery framing (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) because a citation for physiology or medicine is best anchored in what was discovered about the hormone, with the drug class as its demonstrated consequence.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Credit is contested between Mojsov and Habener's group on identification of the active peptide form, Habener is not among the credited names, and any three-person limit omits Knudsen, whose team engineered the long-acting analogues that actually reached patients. Choosing the physiology trio could be read as under-valuing the drug-development step that produced the impact. A prize resting on a disputed priority claim may also be harder to defend than a cleaner configuration such as CAR-T or SMN2 antisense.

responses.point: Svenningsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Knudsen as decisive for translating GLP-1 into long-acting drugs while acknowledging that Mojsov's early peptide work is a real credit question.
responses.response: I take the Knudsen argument seriously, since without liraglutide and semaglutide the biology would not have changed practice. I still place Mojsov third because the prize tradition rewards the discovery that made the development rational, and identification of the active GLP-1 form is such a step, whereas industrial design of acylated analogues is a second achievement. I would accept Knudsen if the committee prefers a drug-centred citation, but then Mojsov's omission needs an explicit defence. A two-part prize combining incretin physiology with analogue development cannot fit within three people without dropping someone.

responses.point: Linnarsson also proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the strongest scientific trio from the supplied names, noting that Knudsen is a plausible alternative and that the Habener group cannot be judged from the text.
responses.response: I agree on the trio, but agreement between two members is not evidence that the priority question is resolved. Identification of GLP-1(7-36) as the active form was reported by more than one group, and our supplied list does not carry Habener. I would want the committee to say explicitly that Mojsov's inclusion rests on the peptide chemistry and characterization contribution and not on first discovery of the hormone, and to test that against the primary literature before relying on it.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics third and asks whether a research tool fits the prize's expectation of benefit to human health, and flags that six credited names far exceed three places.
responses.response: I share both concerns, and they are why I rank B033 only sixth. The tool changed causal neuroscience, but credit among Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg, Deisseroth, Boyden and Miesenboeck is crowded, and the clinical payoff is still at an early stage. I disagree with placing it above CAR-T, where the clinical proof is firm. I accept that it is exceptionally original and widely adopted, so ranking it lower reflects attribution and maturity of benefit, not weak science.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks BCR-ABL inhibition second, calling the attribution comparatively clean (Lydon, Druker, Sawyers) and the concept, compound and clinical proof all clear.
responses.response: The attribution is cleaner than for GLP-1, and I agree the paradigm is important. My reservation is that this is largely a drug-development achievement whose upstream discovery (the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL fusion) is not credited, and the central figures have already been recognized with major prizes. I therefore rank it below CAR-T and SMN2 antisense, where the conceptual novelty at the time was higher. I would reconsider if the committee decides the targeted-therapy paradigm is still unrecognized and a clean trio is the priority.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks optogenetics second and the unfolded protein response fourth, treating methods-based impact and mechanism-based basic science as legitimate prize material even without a large therapeutic payoff.
responses.response: I agree that the UPR is a clean, original two-person case and rank it fourth for that reason, and that a Nobel does not require therapeutic translation. Where I differ is on optogenetics, which I rank below CAR-T and SMN2 antisense mainly because of unresolved credit among six people; a clean prize needs a defensible three-person split, which GLP-1 only partly achieves and optogenetics does not.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution is the identification of the active peptide form or a priority claim shared with Habener's group, which I cannot settle from the supplied text.
Whether the committee prefers the basic-physiology strand or the drug-development strand (Knudsen) within a three-person limit.
Whether CAR-T with June and Sadelain, or SMN2 antisense with Krainer and Bennett, offers a cleaner attribution than GLP-1 if the credit dispute cannot be resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from the provided profile. I disclose a field interest in RNA processing and splicing relevant to B007 (SMN2) and B042 (Ire1/Hac1 splicing), and past co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen, but none of the credited candidates appears connected to me personally; shared topic or institution does not by itself require recusal.
